OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify common musculoskeletal disorders associated with myelomeningocele.
Assess a patient’s neurologic level and associated musculoskeletal manifestations.
Understand the common complications associated with myelomeningocele.
Implement surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for patients with myelomeningocele.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Myelodysplasia/spina bifida disorders include a spectrum of congenital malformations of the
spinal column and the spinal cord resulting from failure of the neural crest (neural tube) to
close at 3 to 4 weeks after fertilization.1

Spina bifida occulta is the failure of posterior bony spinal elements to fuse, but it causes no
neurologic impairment.
Epidemiology
Myelomeningocele is the most common major birth defect, occurring in 0.9 per 1,000 live
births.1
Prenatal diagnosis is made via assay of alpha-fetoprotein concentration in maternal serum.1
The diagnosis also can be made via ultrasonography or by amniocentesis.
Women of childbearing age should be encouraged to consume a diet with adequate folic acid
intake (eg, the vitamin is added to many foods, such as breads and cereals). Supplementation
with folic acid decreases the risk of spina bifida but only if taken during the first weeks after
conception.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
In patients with meningocele, the dura and tissue overlying the spinal cord pouch out through
the bony defect; however, the spinal cord remains within the spinal canal, typically causing
little neurologic impairment.
In patients with myelomeningocele, overlying tissues and the spinal cord are not contained by
the unfused posterior bony spine elements. The neural elements are covered in a pouch of
skin or only dura or are entirely exposed. This may cause major motor and sensory deficits.
Nerves
Spina bifida most frequently occurs in the lumbosacral region of the spine, but it also can
involve the thoracic level.
The most distal functioning level determines function.
Quadriceps function, or L4, is an important differentiator for function because it implies active
quadriceps function. Adults without active quadriceps function have difficulty ambulating in
the community.2

Nerves

In patients with spina bifida, the level of the lesion is an important indicator of prognosis.
For example, patients with a thoracic level lesion will universally use wheelchairs for
independent mobility. Although quadriceps function is a critical predictor of household
and community ambulation, hip reduction or dislocation is not associated with
ambulatory capacity.3
Etiology
Spina bifida results from failure of the neural tube to close during the fourth week of
embryogenesis.
Natural History
Predicting the functional level of a child with myelomeningocele immediately after birth is
difficult because injury to the neural elements may be partial or complete regardless of the
level of the lesion.4
Continued clinical examinations and bracing as needed often are helpful until a child’s
functional level becomes clear.
Quadriceps function often can be assessed in a newborn, but the strength grade may be
difficult to determine.
Most affected children benefit from multidisciplinary care, including neurosurgery for
associated hydrocephalus, Arnold-Chiari malformations, and a tethered cord. Given the high
incidence of bowel and bladder dysfunction associated with spina bifida, many patients also
benefit from consultation with a pediatric urologist.5

Natural History
Typically, a neurologic lesion and its level are static in patients with spina bifida.
However, function may worsen in patients with a tethered cord, for which spina bifida is
a risk factor.
Risk Factors

Previously affected pregnancy
Low folic acid intake
Pregestational maternal diabetes mellitus
In utero exposure to valproic acid or carbamazepine1
Classification
Spina bifida is classified based on the level of the lesion5 (Table 1).
Neural integrity at the L4 level or lower (active quadriceps muscle function) is considered
necessary for ambulation in the community.4 An iliopsoas strength of 0 to 3 is a strong
predictor of reliance on a wheelchair.6

Classification
Spina bifida is classified based on the level of the lesion. Group 1 lesions occur at the
thoracic or high-lumbar level. Affected patients do not have quadriceps function and
require a wheelchair for independent mobility. Group 2 lesions occur at the low-lumbar
level. Affected patients retain quadriceps and medial hamstring function but lack gluteus
medius and maximus function. Most of these children will maintain ambulatory capacity
as adults by using crutches and braces. Finally, patients with group 3 lesions have
quadriceps and hip abductor function and tend to be community ambulators with the
use of a below-knee brace.6
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Spina bifida is most often diagnosed during routine prenatal ultrasonography.
The risk of associated genetic anomalies is increased in patients with spina bifida.
Physical Examination
Latex-free gloves must be used for physical examination or procedures in children with spina
bifida because of the increased risk of type 1 hypersensitivity resulting in anaphylaxis.7
Newborns should be assessed for contractures and foot deformities, such as clubfoot or
vertical tali.8

Imaging Studies
Most diagnoses of spina bifida are made via prenatal ultrasonography.
Diagnosis
Genetic diagnoses often are associated with spina bifida.
A multidisciplinary team and referral for genetic evaluation often are helpful.
Differential Diagnosis
Spina bifida is most often diagnosed via prenatal ultrasonography; however, several other
pathologies may present a similar clinical picture. They include early childhood and perinatal
spinal cord tumors and spinal cord injury or infarct.
Management
The long-term medical and skeletal issues associated with myelomeningocele often are best
addressed by a multidisciplinary team.
Nonsurgical Management
Frequent skin checks for pressure sores and well-fitting braces and wheelchairs are important
in the management of myelomeningocele because complete lack of sensation often is present
in the distal lower extremities.
Urologic and gastrointestinal issues, including detrusor malfunction and abnormal sphincter
tone, require early catheterization and bowel regimens. Kidney reflux and pyelonephritis may
cause substantial morbidity and mortality in patients with myelomeningocele.
Carefully recorded neurologic examinations are crucial because late issues requiring
neurosurgery are common (eg, tethering, syrinx, and shunt problems).
Latex allergies are common in patients with myelomeningocele, necessitating the use of latex-
free gloves and equipment during treatment.
For optimal physical function, rehabilitation should include early mobilization, physical
therapy, bracing, and wheelchair fitting.
Bracing

6/14

In patients with myelomeningocele, hip-knee-ankle-foot orthoses, knee-ankle-foot orthoses,
or ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) frequently are used to support stance and/or prevent
contracture.
As the child grows and gains skills, bracing and crutch requirements may decrease; however,
if weight gain or deformity occur, these requirements may increase.
Pathologic Fracture
Children with spina bifida have a higher risk of fracture and delayed diagnosis of fractures.9
In immobile children without sensation, fractures often present as erythema, warmth, and
swelling and may be confused with infection.
Cast immobilization is a typical treatment option; however, the cast should be well padded.
Often, transitioning quickly to a bivalved and lined cast allows for skin checks.
Fractures often heal with an atypical but robust callous pattern in a fusiform shape.10

Pathologic Fracture
Pathologic fractures are very common in patients with spina bifida because of a lack of
weight bearing. Similar to any other child, cast immobilization generally is an acceptable
treatment option; however, the cast should be well padded. If the patient is undergoing
surgical fixation for the management of fractures, bone quality may be poor, and fixed
angle implants may be helpful. 
Skin Ulceration
Daily skin care and checks should be emphasized from an early age.
Osteomyelitis may be associated with nonhealing ulcers, especially on the calcaneus.11
Amputation may be required to manage chronically nonhealing wounds refractory to medical
and surgical management.12

Skin Ulceration
SEND FEEDBACK

7/14

Skin ulcerations are very common in patients with spina bifida. These wounds are
difficult to manage, and prevention is the most effective form of management. Patients
must be careful if walking barefoot and in water or on rough surfaces. Frequent wearing
of foot protection is essential. In addition, fusion should be avoided during surgical
procedures on the feet because loss of motion segments in the insensate foot promotes
ulceration.8,13
Surgical Management
Spine
Neonates with myelomeningocele are delivered via cesarean section to avoid additional
neurologic damage. Neurosurgical closure of myelomeningocele is performed within 48
hours after delivery, with a shunt used to manage hydrocephalus. Myelomeningoceles also
can be closed prenatally.
In a child with myelomeningocele, tethering of the spinal cord may cause progressive
scoliosis or spasticity or alter functional capabilities.
Syrinx, shunt problems, or new hydrocephalus may cause new symptoms that affect the
upper extremities, such as weakness or increasing spasticity.
In infancy, an Arnold-Chiari malformation often is managed via shunting to control
hydrocephalus but may require subsequent decompression. Later symptoms may include
spasticity or weakness of the lower extremities, problems with swallowing, and absence of a
cough reflex.
Scoliosis and kyphosis may be progressive in patients with myelomeningocele and may
require management via spinal fusion.
Hip
Hip flexion contractures are common in patients with myelomeningocele but often are well
tolerated in children who prefer wheelchair ambulation. In patients with lower lumbar
involvement, contracture exceeding 40° may require flexor muscle release if it interferes with
hygiene or wheelchair seating.
Hip range of motion is more important than imaging appearance.
Hip reduction or dislocation does not correlate with ambulation.14 (Figure 1)
Dysplasia and/or dislocation of the hip occurs in many patients with involvement at the
midlumbar level.

These patients have medial hamstring and quadriceps muscle function but poor hip
extensor and abductor function, causing muscle imbalance that results in hip dysplasia and
instability.
The standard of care is to not reduce a dislocated hip in any child with
myelomeningocele.5,14,15
The exception to nonsurgical management of hip dislocation in children with
myelomeningocele may be unilateral dislocation of the hip in a child with a low-level lesion
(ie, a community ambulator). However, the rate of dislocation recurrence is high, and the
procedure is controversial.5

Knee
In ambulatory children, flexion contracture of the knee exceeding 20° may be managed via
hamstring lengthening, capsular release, growth modulation of the anterior distal femoral
physis, and/or distal femoral extension osteotomy (Figures 2 and 3). However, the
recurrence rate of flexion contracture after extension osteotomy in growing children is
substantial.16
Children with a preference for wheelchair mobility tolerate knee flexion contractures better
than ambulatory children. The threshold for surgical management of these contractures
depends on the child and the family’s desire for household ambulation.
Extension contracture of the knee may be managed via serial cast immobilization or via V-Y
quadriceps lengthening.16 In very young children and newborns, home-based therapy often
may resolve impressive knee extension contractures.
Knee valgus, often with associated external tibial torsion and femoral anteversion, is
common in patients with midlumbar-level myelomeningocele because they lack functional
hip abductors and have a substantial trunk shift when walking with an AFO.17 This may be
addressed with the use of a knee-ankle-foot orthosis or crutches with an AFO.
External tibial torsion may be addressed via a distal tibial derotational osteotomy.

Foot
Approximately 30% of children with myelomeningocele have a rigid clubfoot.18
Although these clubfeet are more rigid, they are amenable to traditional Ponseti cast
immobilization and Achilles tenotomy. However, the risk of recurrence is much higher19
With surgical management, portions of the tendons of the foot (eg, Achilles tendon, tibialis
posterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum communis) may be resected rather than
lengthened to decrease the risk of clubfoot recurrence.8
Equinus contracture is common in patients with thoracic or high lumbar-level
myelomeningocele. In school-aged and older children especially, these contractures often
are driven by capsular tightness, and Achilles tendon lengthening or aponeurotic release is
less effective.

Calcaneal foot position may occur with unopposed contraction of the anterior tibialis muscle
(ie, myelomeningocele affecting the L3-L4 level of the spine).
Equinovarus, equinus, and calcaneal foot deformities often are best managed via a simple
tenotomy rather than tendon transfer, achieving a flail but braceable foot.
Valgus foot deformities are common in patients with myelomeningocele at the L4-L5 level. If
surgical management is necessary to achieve a plantigrade foot, then fusion should be
avoided to maintain foot flexibility and decrease the risk of pressure sores.13
